doc.title: Development Tools
doc.paragraph: This section goes over some of the many tools that will help make development easier. None of these tools are an absolute requirement for development.

section.title: Docker
section.paragraph: Docker is a lightweight virtualization solution, allowing you to containerize software that needs to run in a Linux runtime environment. Windows, MacOS and Linux all provide options to run Docker containers. Visit https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/ for installation and configuration instructions for your Operating System. On Windows, see Windows with WSL 2 below for the setup we have verified.

section.title: Visual Studio Code
section.paragraph: Visual Studio Code, or VS Code, is an IDE created and maintained by Microsoft. It's a powerful editor that uses an extension marketplace to provide additional functionality to its core features. One such feature is Dev Containers, which allows VS Code to interact with Docker. This allows you to setup a custom development environment inside a Docker container. For instructions on installing VS Code, please visit https://code.visualstudio.com/download.

section.title: Open the Repository in the Dev Container
section.paragraph: The repository includes a Dev Container configuration (.devcontainer). It builds a container with all of the tools you need for development, the same environment we use and test with. Clone the repository onto a Linux file system, check out the develop branch, and open the folder in VS Code:
section.code: git clone https://github.com/afw-org/afw.git cd afw git checkout develop code .
section.paragraph: Then, from the Command Palette (Show All Commands), select Dev Containers: Reopen in Container. The first time, Docker downloads and builds the development image, which can take a while.

At the time of this writing, current development, including the Dev Container configuration, is on develop, and GitHub's default branch, main, is behind it. For now, check out develop before opening the container.

The container bind-mounts the folder that holds your clone (the clone's parent folder) at /workspaces, so the repository is at /workspaces/afw, and anything you clone next to it, such as your own extensions, is there too. Your files and git history stay on the host: rebuilding or deleting the container does not touch them.
Where to put the clone:

list.item: Linux: anywhere, for example in your home directory.

MacOS: anywhere. Docker Desktop shares host folders with the container through virtiofs, which makes a bind-mounted clone fast. Older Docker Desktop releases made bind mounts slow on MacOS, which is why this guide used to recommend a Docker volume instead.

Windows: inside a WSL 2 Linux distribution, for example ~/afw in Ubuntu. Do not clone onto the Windows file system (a Windows folder, or /mnt/c from WSL): the container is slow on it, and a clone made by Git for Windows can have Windows line endings. See Windows with WSL 2 below.

section.title: Windows with WSL 2
section.paragraph: The setup we have verified on Windows runs Docker Engine inside WSL 2 Ubuntu, with Docker Desktop uninstalled. VS Code itself runs on Windows and reaches the clone through its WSL extension. Docker Desktop with its WSL 2 backend and a clone on the WSL file system should also work, but has not been tried.

steps.step: In an Ubuntu terminal, install Docker Engine: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh then sudo sh get-docker.sh.
Let your user run Docker: sudo groupadd docker (the group may already exist), then sudo usermod -aG docker $USER.
If your home directory is now owned by root, give it back: sudo chown -R $USER:$USER $HOME.
From PowerShell, run wsl --shutdown so the group change takes effect, then open a new Ubuntu terminal.
Clone the repository, check out develop and run code . as shown above, then select Dev Containers: Reopen in Container.

section.paragraph: If ./afwdev fails with not found, the file was checked out with Windows (CRLF) line endings, so its #!/bin/sh line names an interpreter that does not exist. Clone inside WSL instead, or, in an existing clone, run rm afwdev then git checkout afwdev to check it out again with Linux line endings.

section.title: The First Build
section.paragraph: In the container's terminal, build and install everything, then run the tests:
For day-to-day C work, ./afwdev build --cdev is quicker: it builds and installs the C runtime, the extensions and afwdev, but not the documentation or the administrative web application.

section.title: What the Build Options Do
section.paragraph: afwdev build works in one or more contexts: --cmake for the C code (the default when you name no context), --docs for this handbook and the Doxygen pages, --js for the JavaScript packages and the administrative web application, and --docker for the Docker images. Other options, such as --generate, --clean and --install, apply to each context you choose. --clean only cleans those contexts, so --docs --clean leaves the C build alone.
You will rarely need to put these together yourself, because two options do it for you:

row.column: --all --generate --clean --install --scan -j: the C code, the docs and the JavaScript, plus the clang static analyzer.

section.paragraph: Note that --all by itself only selects the C, docs and JavaScript contexts. It does not generate or install. Neither --all nor --fulldev builds the Docker images: that means a full C build for each platform, which is slow, so pass --docker only when you want them.

Both --cdev and --fulldev compile in debugging support (AFW_DEBUG_EVALUATION, AFW_DEBUG_LOCK and AFW_DEBUG_POOL; each stays off at run time until you turn it on), and AFW_VALGRIND_POOL when the valgrind headers are installed, so valgrind can see inside pools. You can add your own C defines with --define NAME or --define NAME=VALUE, as many times as you need.

--sanitize address and --sanitize thread build the C code with AddressSanitizer or ThreadSanitizer into a tree of their own (build/asan/cmake/ or build/tsan/cmake/). That build is never installed; afwdev test --env-mode asan or tsan runs the tests against it.
Use ./afwdev, from the package root, for a build that may install a new afwdev. After that, the afwdev on your PATH is current.

section.title: Clone into a Container Volume
section.paragraph: If you would rather not keep a clone on the host, VS Code can clone the repository into a Docker volume. The source then lives only in that volume: host tools cannot see it, and deleting the volume deletes your work.

steps.step: From the Command Palette, select Dev Containers: Clone Repository in Named Container Volume...
Enter the repository URL, https://github.com/afw-org/afw.git. VS Code clones GitHub's default branch (currently main).
Create a new volume or choose an existing one, and accept the default repository name afw.
When the container is running, run git checkout develop in its terminal, then select Dev Containers: Rebuild Container so the container is built from the develop configuration.

section.title: Using the VS Code Tasks
section.paragraph: Once the development Docker Container is running, you can do anything manually, from the built-in terminal that VS Code provides. In addition, there are various VS Code "tasks" that are available to perform many of these steps.

section.title: Creating a Multi-Root Workspace
section.paragraph: If you plan to develop extensions or applications, outside of the afw core folder, you may want to create a workspace to contain both core and your extensions and apps.

Clone those repositories next to afw, so they share its parent folder. In the container they appear under /workspaces. With a container volume, clone them into /workspaces from the container's terminal.
Then select File -> Save Workspace As... from the menu bar and save the workspace file (afw.code-workspace by default) outside of all of your repository folders, for example in /workspaces.
Once you have saved the workspace, you can add additional project repository folders to your workspace by using the File -> Add Folder to Workspace... command.
